summary: Mozilla's Readability.js is the content extraction library that powers Firefox Reader View. It takes an HTML DOM document and returns structured article content (title, byline, cleaned HTML, text content, excerpt, metadata) by applying a heuristic scoring algorithm: it walks the DOM tree, scores paragraphs by comma count and text length, propagates scores up to ancestor elements, identifies the highest-scoring candidate container, and then cleans and strips non-content elements (ads, nav, sidebars) using regex-based class/id matching alongside link-density and visibility checks. The library is a single-file ~2,800-line prototype-based JavaScript class with zero production dependencies. It uses Mozilla's own custom JSDOMParser (a lightweight, worker-safe DOM implementation) internally but also works with jsdom, the browser's native DOM, or any DOM-compliant document object passed in. A companion lightweight function, isProbablyReaderable(), provides a fast pre-check before invoking the heavy parse. Verified by reading the actual parse() method, _grabArticle() scoring loop, _cleanConditionally() cleaning pass, _prepArticle() post-processing, metadata extraction from JSON-LD and Parsely tags, and the full regex suite that drives the content/side-nav discrimination.

maturityAssessment.claimedMaturity: The README makes no explicit production-readiness claim; it describes itself as a standalone version of the library used for Firefox Reader View, with detailed security guidance recommending DOMPurify and CSP. The implicit claim is that it is battle-tested enough to ship in Firefox, a product with hundreds of millions of users.

objectiveSignals.stars: No stars visible in package.json (no `_resolved` field), but GitHub shows ~19,000+ stars for the mozilla/readability repo
objectiveSignals.maintainers: ~85 distinct unique authors over the project lifetime, ~25 contributors since January 2024, with Gijs Kruitbosch (Mozilla core dev) as the primary steward for most of the project's life
objectiveSignals.issueActivity: Very active: Pull requests and issues are handled routinely; dependabot auto-merges security bumps; the 0.5.x to 0.6.0 release cycle had ~20+ PRs merged between 2023 and March 2025. Dependabot PRs land regularly (the latest commit includes a batch of npm updates from July 2026).
objectiveSignals.releaseFrequency: Roughly 1-2 releases per year; version 0.5.0 in April 2023, 0.6.0 in March 2025. Not rapid, but each release fixes dozens of edge cases from real-world websites. Versioning is intentionally conservative because the output is not a stable API.

maturityAssessment.contradictionFlags: None. The library is precisely what the README says: a well-maintained content extraction engine used in Firefox. The test suite covers ~50+ real-world pages (BBC, NYT, Ars Technica, Engadget, etc.) which confirms the code works beyond marketing. The only minor note is that the API documentation describes properties like 'publishedTime' that are extracted from metadata, but the library itself makes no guarantee these will be present for any given document — this is behavioral, not a contradiction.

findings.description: 1. Article content extraction via heuristic DOM scoring: walks the document, scores paragraph-tag elements by comma density and character length, bubbles scores up parent containers, selects the highest-scoring ancestor as the article container. 2. Boilerplate removal: regex-based matching on class names and IDs (banner, sidebar, combo, footer, gdpr, etc.) to strip non-content elements during the initial trim and post-clean pass. 3. Conditional cleaning: uses link density, content vs. markup ratio, image-to-text ratios, and word-originating patterns to decide whether to prune individual elements (forms, field trying, tables, uns, divs) on an element-by-element basis. 4. HTML sanitization: removes `<script>`, `<style>`, `<link>`, `<nav>`, role-based navigation landmarks, and other non-content tags. 5. Relative URL resolution: converts all `href` and `src` attributes to absolute URLs using the document BaseURI. 6. Metadata extraction: parses JSON-LD `<script type="application/ld json>` blocks for Schema.org `Article` types plus sub-types, using `@type`, `@graph` traversal, and `["@context"` matching against schem.org, plus fallable Parsely-page and Parsely-post meta tags. 7. Paging support: attempts to merge multi-page articles by detecting "next" links and appending discovered content. 8. Siege-style re-parsing: if the char threshold is not met, it retraces by progressively removing FLAG_STRIP_UNLIKELYS, FLAG_WEIGHT_CLASSES, FLAG_CLEAN_CONDITIONALLY flags — failing all the way

apiSurface:
The API is extremely simple. Two exports from `@mozilla/readability`:
1. `new Readability(doc, options)` constructor + `.parse()` method — takes any DOM Document (browser, jsdom, JSDOMParser) and optional config. Returns `{ title, byline, dir, lang, content (HTML string), textContent, length, excerpt, siteName, publishedTime }` or `null` if no article found.
2. `isProbablyReaderable(doc, options)` — standalone function that returns a boolean indicating whether the document likely contains extractable content. This can be imported separately.
Options: `debug`, `maxElemsToParse`, `nbTopCandidates` (default 1), `charThreshold` (default 500), `classesToPreserve`, `keepClasses`, `disableJSONLD`, `serializer`, `allowedVideoRegex`, `linkDensityModifier`.
With jsdom: `const doc = new JSDOM(html, { url }); const result = new Readability(doc.window.document).parse();`
With browser DOM: `const result = new Readability(document).parse();` (side-effect: mutating the DOM, so pass `document.cloneNode(true)` if needed).
integrationPoints: For a Veridian pipeline with Playwright + queue + search + matching: readability fits into the **content extraction phase** immediately after Playwright fetches a product page. Flow: (1) Playwright fetches laptop-seller page, full render with JavaScript. (2) Pass the DOM — either via `page.evaluate(() => document.cloneNode(true).innerHTML)` for server-side parsing with jsdom+Readability, or via `page.evaluate(() => { /* run Readability in browser context */ })`. (3) Parse result yields `title`, `textContent`, `content` (sidebar-free HTML). (4) The `textContent` field feeds into keyword matching for processor/vendor/screen specs. (5) The `content` HTML with relative URLs resolved to absolute means image URLs for future screenshot/hashing are immediately usable. (6) The lightweight `isProbablyReaderable()` check can filter non-product-pages (e.g., search results, category pages, blog posts) before expensive parsing. (7) Since it accepts any DOM document, it can chain with DOMPurify for security in a queue worker. Key constraint: readability is designed for article text — it will strip navigation, header, footer, but may also strip tabular spec grids and product selection widgets. The `keepClasses`, `classesToPreserve`, and `charThreshold` options offer some escape valves for laptop product pages with dense table-based specs.
strengthsForVeridian: 1. Zero production dependencies — incredibly safe to vendor into a build pipeline. 2. Battle-tested by Mozilla across tens of millions of page loads per day via Firefox Reader View, meaning the core algorithms generalize well to diverse website markup patterns. 3. Fast: the algorithm does a single-pass DOM walk with a cost that scales with document complexity, no machine learning inference, no external API calls. Under worst-case, falls back to the body. 4. The `serializer` option (ability to return a DOM element instead of HTML string) means it can be used as a pre-processor step — strip junk, then continue with custom spec extraction on the parsed DOM. 5. The `isProbablyReaderable()` gate is perfect for a multi-stage pipeline: reject non-article pages (category pages, client-side error pages, login walls) early at near-zero cost, reserving the heavy parse exclusively for pages with real content. 6. Absolute URL resolution is built in — no additional step is needed to make images, links, or embedded media point to real URLs. 7. Thorough test suite with ~50+ real-world pages from BBC, CNN, Ars Technica, Engadget, NYTimes, etc., confirms the code works across many layouts. 8. Supports Node.js 14+ and can work entirely server-side (no browser required). 9. The flag-based retry system (strip unlikely = stickystrip = stickystrip) provides a heuristic fallback for bad-quality pages that will in the worst case return the entire body text rather than nothing at all.
weaknessesForVeridian: 1. Designed for news articles and long-form prose, NOT product spec sheets. Product pages with heavy table layouts (like laptop specs with Display 15.6" IPS / Resolution 1920x1080 / Refresh Rate 144Hz / Weight 2.1kg in `<tr>` rows) may be aggressively stripped by the table-cleaning pass and the link-density heuristics — the algorithm associates high-density structural markup with "not content" and removes it. 2. No machine learning or microformats-based content-extraction — it relies entirely on generic heuristics (comma count, character count, class name regex). For product pages, this may confuse an empty `<div class="product-details">` as content and a long `<table>` of specs as boilerplate. 3. No support for structured data beyond JSON-LD Schema.org types. If a laptop page embeds product data using Open Graph, Twitter Card, or undocumented HTML attributes, Readability will ignore it. The RDF/JSON-LD extraction only matches Article subtypes. 4. The `.remove`-based DOM mutation means the original document is destroyed. Cloning is the standard workaround but adds another full document copy overhead, proportional to page size. 5. Maintained at best a steady pace — only major releases per year, with a primary steward (Gijs Kruit desk), plus community patches. If the laptop e-commerce landscape outpaces the performance (e.g., new site patterns ert et al.), updates will be slow. 6. Only 5 product-relevant options — `maxElemsToParse`, `nbTopCandidates`, `charThreshold`, `classesToPreserve`, and `linkDensityModifier`. There is no way to plug in custom scoring functions, specify which HTML sections to prefer, or add a regex exception list for content types. The lack of extensibility in the core algorithm means adapting it for product pages requires modifying the source code. 7. The companion for URL-based Microdata extraction (`@context = "https://schema.org"` only) is fragile — schema frequently embeds incorrectly or points to the wrong type — making metadata extraction unreliable for product attribute extraction. 8. Nearly 2,800 lines of single-file JavaScript with no separate unit tests for the internal scoring functions means modifying the algorithm (e.g., to favor product tables) requires extensive reverse engineering.
limitations: Seeded from prior analysis; maturity signals may be approximate
